Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: This item appears misclassified within the Threat node because it describes an avoidance behaviour rather than a threat appraisal or sense of current danger. Given the formulation, the only active link is Threat → Maladaptive Strategies, so threat items should plausibly drive coping responses; this item itself is already a maladaptive strategy and duplicates the behavioural content of the Maladaptive Strategies node. The other Threat items (flashbacks, scanning exits) reflect re-experiencing/current danger more coherently for torture trauma.

vignette:
Priya is a 28-year-old South Asian woman who works as a tailor out of a small studio attached to her home, where she and her husband share a modest but carefully kept life. She was referred for psychological assessment following persistent concerns raised by her husband, who had noticed a marked deterioration in her functioning over the preceding months. Her PCL-5 score of 69 places her firmly in the severe range of post-traumatic stress, and the picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions was one of a woman whose internal world had been fundamentally reorganized around the anticipation of danger.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Priya was detained by authorities during a period of civil unrest in her country of origin, which she had returned to briefly to visit family. What followed over the course of several days was a systematic experience of torture - prolonged physical restraint, threats delivered in close proximity, and the particular helplessness of being confined in a room from which there was no visible exit and no way to predict what would come next. She was eventually released without charge. She returned to the United States, told almost no one what had happened, and attempted to resume her life.

The resumption did not hold. Within weeks, Priya found that the studio where she worked - the small, windowless back room where she cut and stitched fabric - had become nearly intolerable. The click of a door latch, the muffled sounds of the street outside, the particular quality of stillness in an enclosed space: these sensations carried her back with a force that felt less like memory and more like recurrence. She would be mid-seam and then, without transition, she was there again - the room, the restraints, the proximity of threat - and her body would respond as though no time had passed at all. These flashbacks were not experienced as recollections. She was certain, in those moments, that something was happening to her now.

It was this quality of present-tense danger that shaped almost everything that followed. The threat she felt was not abstract or anticipatory - it was immediate and embodied, and it demanded a response. From the moment she entered any room, including her own studio, Priya found herself cataloguing exits: the door behind her, the window to the left, whether the latch opened inward or out. She was superalert in a way that exhausted her but that she could not voluntarily suspend, scanning faces, monitoring sounds, reading the air of any space for signs of what might come. This sustained state of hypervigilance, and the flashbacks that erupted through it, together formed the engine of her avoidance. Because the threat felt so real and so close, Priya had come to believe that the only reasonable response was to reduce every possible avenue through which it might arrive.

She stopped attending medical appointments, including a follow-up she had been due for a minor but monitored condition. The idea of a clinical setting - the closed rooms, the vulnerability of examination, the loss of control over her own body - was indistinguishable, in her nervous system, from what she had survived. She avoided situations that might produce strong emotion of any kind, understanding, in her own terms, that feeling anything intensely made her less able to monitor her surroundings. Most strikingly, she had stopped allowing herself to rest. Relaxation, she had concluded, was not safe - to soften her vigilance even briefly was to court the kind of unreadiness that had made her vulnerable before. She sat at her sewing machine for hours without breaks, not from industry but from the belief that stillness invited harm.

The consequence in her work had been slow but accumulating. Clients had begun to notice delays, small errors, a distraction in her manner that had not been there before. One long-standing customer, a woman who had brought her daughter's wedding alterations, had quietly taken the work elsewhere. Her husband, gentle and increasingly worried, had finally persuaded her to seek help - not by arguing that she was unwell, but by telling her he was frightened of losing her to something he could not see. What Priya most hoped for, she said in their second session, was to be able to sit in her studio with the door closed and feel nothing more than the fabric under her hands.
